title: How to remove guidelines from cross-stitch
subtitle: Taking out basting threads and grid lines after the design is complete
excerpt: Guidelines — basting threads used to mark the centre of the design or to create a visible grid on the Aida — need to be removed after stitching is complete. Basting threads are pulled out individually from the back. Fabric marker lines are removed with cold water. Pencil lines are removed by pressing. Each method leaves the Aida clean and undamaged.
sourceNotes: Guideline removal for cross-stitch. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.
The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: Guidelines are temporary markers added to the
before stitching to help with counting. They are usually basting threads (in a contrasting colour to the
and the Aida), or light marks made with a water-erasable fabric marker or pencil. All guidelines must be removed before the piece is framed.

For basting thread guidelines: turn the piece over and find the basting thread runs on the back. Cut the basting thread at the end of each run using small scissors, then pull the short lengths out from the front with tweezers or a tapestry needle. Do not pull the full length through from the back; pulling a long thread through can catch on existing stitches.

Work along the basting thread run, cutting and pulling out each short section in turn until the entire thread is removed. Check from the front that no basting loops remain caught under the cross-stitches.

For water-erasable fabric marker lines: dampen a clean cloth with cold water and dab it over the marked lines. The marker ink dissolves in water and wipes away cleanly. Do not use hot water or an iron while marker lines are still present; heat can set some markers permanently.

Allow the fabric to dry naturally after marker removal, then press from the back. Check from the front in good light that the marks are fully removed before pressing; pressing with heat can fix any remaining marker.

For light pencil marks: press the piece from the back with a damp cloth and warm iron. Light pencil on Aida usually disappears with pressing. If traces remain, a soft eraser on the dry fabric surface after pressing will lift the residue without damaging the weave.

items.symptom: Basting thread is caught under finished stitches and won't come out cleanly
items.cause: The basting thread was stitched through the same holes as the cross-stitches, locking it in place.
items.fix: Use a tapestry needle to work the basting thread end carefully out from under the cross-stitches, cutting it into shorter sections if needed. Do not pull forcefully; this could distort the finished stitches. Work slowly from one end to the other.

items.symptom: Water-erasable marker lines are still visible after dampening
items.cause: The fabric was not wet enough, or the marker lines were old and set.
items.fix: Soak the affected area in cold water for several minutes rather than dabbing. Fresh air-erasable markers sometimes need longer exposure to moisture. If lines remain after soaking, repeat with fresh cold water. Never iron until the lines are completely gone.

content.text: Basting thread in a bright contrasting colour is the most reliable guideline for cross-stitch because it is clearly visible while stitching and comes out without any chemicals or pressing. Use a colour that is distinct from both the Aida and the cross-stitch threads so the guidelines are easy to spot and distinguish from the finished stitches.
